sections.heading: Three registers
sections.body:
French changes noticeably with the situation. Three broad registers (*les registres de langue*):

*Soutenu* is for formal writing, speeches and very polite situations; *courant* is right almost everywhere; *familier* is normal among friends but inappropriate at work or in an exam.

sections.heading: How people really speak
sections.body:
In informal spoken French:

- the ***ne*** of negation is usually dropped: *Je sais pas.* *C'est pas grave.* *Il vient pas.*
- ***on*** replaces *nous*: *On y va ?*
- ***ça*** replaces *cela*: *Ça marche.*
- ***il y a*** becomes *y a*: *Y a du monde !*
- **schwas disappear** and words shrink: *je suis* → /ʃɥi/, *je ne sais pas* → /ʃɛ.pa/, *tu as* → *t'as*, *il* → /i/ before a consonant: *il vient* /i.vjɛ̃/
- questions use intonation, rarely inversion: *Tu viens ?* rather than *Viens-tu ?*

You don't need to speak like this — but you need to **understand** it, because it's what you'll hear in films, on the street and among friends.

sections.heading: Choosing the right register
sections.body: At work, in an exam, with someone you don't know: *courant* or *soutenu*. Write *Je ne sais pas*, never *J'sais pas*. With friends, sprinkling a few *familier* words makes you sound natural — but some words (*vulgaire*) are offensive; when in doubt, don't.

examples: Je ne sais pas ce qu'il veut.
I don't know what he wants. (standard)
Y a du monde ce soir !
There are loads of people tonight!
That makes no difference to me at all. (formal)
Je m'en fiche, fais ce que tu veux.
I don't care, do what you like. (informal)
Je n'ai pas assez d'argent. — J'ai pas assez de fric.
I don't have enough money. (standard — informal)
Dans un mail professionnel, on évite le registre familier.
In a work email, you avoid informal language.
